angle: Five labs shipped the same product in seven weeks: an always-on agent with its own computer that signs into your tools. Why they are all racing for it, what a $300 agent stack genuinely replaces, and the work it does not touch — from someone with nine of these running inside client businesses.

items.title: Introducing dots
items.summary: OpenAI announcing dots itself on 29 September 2026 — the primary source. Always-on personal agents powered by GPT-6 Astra, each on its own cloud computer, working in the background on user-defined goals with minimal oversight. They connect to more than 4,000 apps and are reachable through Slack and Teams. Rollout began for Pro users outside the EEA, Switzerland and the UK, and for Business Premium users across supported regions.

items.title: OpenAI launches Dots, its bubbly agentic avatar
items.summary: Independent coverage of the dots launch on 29 September 2026, confirming the always-on, own-cloud-computer design and the rollout tiers.

items.title: Meta is expanding its AI agent Muse to small businesses
items.summary: On 29 September 2026 — the same day OpenAI launched dots — Meta extended Muse to small businesses, adding integrations including Shopify, Dropbox and Slack. This is the one of the five aimed squarely at the kind of business that runs its own ads.

items.title: Meta debuts Muse, its long-planned personal AI agent
items.summary: Meta launched Muse on 8 September 2026: a personal AI agent that connects to at least six categories of someone's digital life — email, calendar, payments, health, shopping and smart home — and works through multi-step goals with minimal supervision. Three tiers: free, Power at $20 a month, Maximum at $100 a month.

items.title: Grok Bot: What SpaceXAI's New AI Teammate Means for the Agent Race
items.summary: On 11 August 2026 SpaceXAI launched Grok Bot in beta: always-on AI teammates that run on a cloud computer, sign into the tools you already use, and keep working after you have closed the laptop — coming back only when something needs a human decision. Onboarding is by demonstration rather than configuration: a Bot watches you do a task once, recording up to ten minutes with no audio, and turns it into a draft skill you review and test. At launch it was limited to SuperGrok Heavy, Cursor Ultra and Cursor Teams Premium subscribers, on macOS, Windows and iPhones running iOS 18 or later. The same piece names the field: OpenAI has ChatGPT Work, Anthropic has Claude Cowork, Google has Gemini Spark — the same bet from four labs before Meta and dots made it six products from five labs. It also notes the pricing pattern: each of these rides on top of an existing subscription rather than carrying a separate price of its own. items.title: SpaceXAI
items.summary: The company behind Grok is SpaceXAI, not xAI. SpaceX acquired xAI in an all-stock merger in February 2026, valuing xAI at $250 billion, and the combined entity rebranded as SpaceXAI in July 2026. Grok kept its name, pricing and API. Worth stating correctly: most casual coverage still writes xAI.

items.title: Helping small businesses put AI to work
items.summary: OpenAI's own post, 30 September 2026, the day after dots launched, on putting AI to work in small businesses. Primary source, and evidence that the small-business segment is now the contested ground rather than an afterthought.

items.title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei Predicts the First Billion-Dollar Solopreneur by 2026
items.summary: Asked directly at Anthropic’s Code with Claude developer conference, Dario Amodei put a 70-80% probability on the first billion-dollar one-employee company appearing in 2026, and named three likely categories: proprietary trading, developer tools, and businesses built around automated customer service. Note what those three have in common — the product IS software or a decision loop. None has to make, ship or physically serve anything.

items.title: The One-Person Company Is Real in 2026 — But Here’s Where Solo Founders Hit a Wall
items.summary: 36.3% of new ventures in 2026 were solo-founded. A solo founder’s agent stack runs about $300-500 a month in subscriptions against $80,000-120,000 a month for the equivalent human functions. The limits are specific and consistent: market validation, strategic pricing, high-stakes customer judgment and any call requiring genuine founder accountability are not reliably delegable. Agents execute defined processes well and reason poorly when the rules are not yet clear. What stays human: taste and curation — deciding what is worth building — trust and relationship building, and overall strategy.

items.title: Solo Founders Lean On AI To Replace Teams, But Limits Remain
items.summary: Corroborates the pattern: solo operators are genuinely replacing team functions with agents, and the limits are real rather than temporary. A final human review on anything going to a customer, partner or press contact is treated as non-negotiable — not because agents cannot write, but because a voice under pressure is not reliably reproducible.
